title: Why ice floats
text: Almost every substance is denser as a solid than as a liquid, so its solid form simply {{1}} in its own melt. Water, mercifully, is the exception: ice floats. The reason lies in the {{2}} shape of the water molecule, whose hydrogen bonds lock into a hexagonal lattice as the liquid cools, holding the molecules further apart than before; ice is about nine per cent less dense than the water {{3}} it. The consequences run far beyond ice cubes. Because floating ice {{4}} the surface, lakes freeze from the top downwards, leaving a liveable layer of four-degree water below in which fish {{5}} the winter; if water behaved like other liquids, ponds would freeze solid from the bottom up and aquatic life would have to {{6}} from nothing every spring. The same principle shapes the planet: sea ice reflects sunlight, slowing climate change, and the polar ice sheets exist only because each summer's melt never quite {{7}} the winter's snowfall. It is strange to reflect that the behaviour of one small molecule {{8}} whether a pond has fish in it at all.

gaps.explanation: 'its solid form sinks in its own melt' — goes below the surface; soak and spill do not take this intransitive sense, stall = stop.
'the angular shape of the molecule' — bent, with a corner; annual = yearly, ample = plentiful.
'less dense than the water beneath it' — directly below; beside = next to, between needs two objects.
'floating ice seals the surface' — closes it like a lid; stir = mix, stain = discolour.
'in which fish survive the winter' — live through it; starve and shiver would make the layer deadly, contradicting the point.
'would have to begin from nothing every spring' — start again; belong takes no 'from' phrase like this, befall means happen to.
'the summer melt never quite exceeds the winter snowfall' — is never greater than; excel = be outstanding, expel = force out.
'the behaviour of one small molecule decides whether a pond has fish' — determines it; deny = declare untrue, divide = separate.
